title: How DataOceans modernize their equity management with Pulley
summary: DataOceans outgrew their complex in-house equity process and needed help migrating to a new system. Pulley answered the call, migrating a complex cap table, assuring for accuracy. Now DataOceans serves its stakeholders with ease and confidence.
body_text: Introduction DataOceans is a leading provider of Customer Communication Management (CCM) solutions catering to over 150 direct and indirect customers, ranging from innovative start-ups to Fortune 500 companies. Their Oceanus CCM Platform provides companies with customer portals for communications across channels, while also offering digitized processes for managing regulatory letter, notices, customer billing and payment processes. Founded in 2004, they’ve grown to an estimated annual revenue of over $10m, built on a remarkable 98% retention rate. DataOceans has firmly established its presence as a partner for managing customer communication, billing, and compliance in highly regulated consumer finance, credit union, banking, and healthcare sectors. They help their customers modernize and digitize a number of legacy processes, so when their cap table management became too manual and difficult, they knew there was a better solution out there. Challenge Larry Buckley, the CEO and Founder of DataOceans, faced a formidable challenge after relying on Excel spreadsheets to manage the company's cap table for more than 18 years. The labor-intensive process of maintaining equity data on spreadsheets was becoming unsustainable. They sought out and engaged another cap table solution, and after a disappointing 6-month attempt at onboarding, the solution failed to set up the cap table accurately. Frustrated with that experience, Buckley nearly gave-up. After doing more research and tapping his network for recommendations, he discovered Pulley. ‍ ‍ Solution After speaking with Pulley's sales team, Larry quickly recognized the potential of the platform to meet DataOceans' specific needs. The value of having a cap table expert onboarding DataOceans to the platform, and then available for support, caught Buckley's attention. A dedicated onboarding specialist ensures a smooth transition The complexity of DataOceans’ cap table was a result of multiple equity sales and unique transactions that occurred over many years. Pulley’s personalized approach proved to be the ideal solution, as Larry worked closely with Pulley’s onboarding specialist to migrate the cap table, eliminating the need for spreadsheets to manage the company’s equity. All stakeholders benefit from having access to equity-holding Previously, stakeholders had low to no awareness of their equity holdings due to the absence of real-time information. Information requests from stakeholders were ad hoc, and manual. Pulley helped to streamline and professionalize communications around holdings to employees and investors. Now, stakeholders can gain access to their latest equity holdings, including vesting schedules, signed documents, and MBO program objectives. These personalized dashboards and access have increased stakeholder engagement and trust. A better 409A experience builds trust Previous 409A processes with other vendors were very manual for Data Oceans. Documents were passed back and forth, the valuation methodology was unclear, with many time-consuming back-and-forth conversations. The choppiness of the process led to a lower confidence in the result. A lack of clear process reduced trust. For DataOcean’s 409As with Pulley, the process was streamlined and simple. They used underlying cap table data, and communicated the process and methodology. Buckley was much happier with the result, and trusted the valuation. ‍ ‍ Making stock incentives more practical DataOceans were managing an internal program for incentives that became unwieldy. One update and the entire program had to be updated. It came to a point where the logistics outweighed the potential benefit, and they considered ending the program. With Pulley they are now able to easily maintain their program. Tasks that previously required extensive manual efforts and coordination among various parties were all streamlined. Stock sales, shareholder list creation, and 409A valuation preparation have all moved online, ensuring compliance with regulatory standards and reducing the risk of errors associated with traditional methods. Results In a short period of time, DataOceans was able to improve the company's cap table management thanks to its collaboration with Pulley: Time savings: Issuing or selling equity used to take weeks; now since everything is electronic, it can be done in days. Risk reduction: Managing these equity tasks online reduced the risk of errors caused by manual processes and physical paperwork. Confidence: The transition from spreadsheets instilled confidence in Larry, allowing him to focus on growth and strategic initiatives. "Managing our cap table was time-consuming, labor-intensive, and frustrating. Pulley has helped us to streamline our cap table management, and gain confidence. We are now able to focus on growth and strategic initiatives, knowing that our cap table is accurate and up-to-date,” said Buckley. If your company is struggling with the administrative burden and complexity of equity management, talk to Pulley cap table expert . Our intuitive platform and best-in-class customer service can help onboard your cap table and streamline your processes, so you and your stakeholders can have a better equity management experience.

title: If Your Value Isn't on the Product Page, Your Only Attribute Is Price
summary: Reps have been told to sell value for 15 years and still lead with price. The problem isn't coaching, it's that the value never made it onto the product page.
body_text: Fifteen years of "sell value, not price" coverage, and reps still open with a number. That's not a coaching failure. The advice targets the sales conversation, and the buying decision increasingly gets made before any conversation happens. If your spec depth, cross-references, technical docs, availability, and service capabilities aren't published where a self-researching buyer (or the AI answering their question) can find them, price is the only attribute you have left to compete on. The advice hasn't changed because the diagnosis was wrong Distribution Strategy Group has been running some version of this argument since at least 2020, when it published "Why Sales Reps Go Straight to Price: 3 Challenges in Selling Value." Five years later, the same outlet was still diagnosing the same failure, this time structurally. "Riding the Distributor Sales Culture into Commodity Hell" argues that sales-driven distributors run 3-5% net operating margin against 8%+ for market-driven competitors, because sellers stay "myopic," pitching the drill instead of the hole it makes. Six months after that, a third piece, "Stop Competing on Price: How Distributors Can Sell Execution Value," arrived with a genuinely useful framework: quantify the cost of an execution failure (a four-hour crew delay at $92/hour runs $2,944; a 3% discount on the same order saves the customer only $600) and coach reps to lead with that math instead of matching the discount. We don't disagree with the math. We disagree with where the fix lives. Three pieces, three sales-side prescriptions, and the underlying commodity problem hasn't moved, because none of it touches what happens before the rep is in the room. Increasingly, nothing happens after, either. The room is empty before the rep gets there Gartner's most recent buyer survey found 67% of B2B buyers now prefer a rep-free purchasing experience . The point of first vendor contact has also been sliding earlier: roughly 69% of the buying journey was complete before a buyer would contact a vendor in 2024; by 2025 that had moved to 61%, per reporting on the shift compiled by Sword and the Script . Forrester's research adds a sharper number still: 48% of first-time B2B buyers already have a preferred vendor in mind before intent signals even register. Whatever a buyer decides during that stretch, they decided it looking at a screen, not a rep. That's the hole in the "sell execution value" prescription. Execution Value (reliable ETAs, pre-approved substitutions, coordinated handoffs) is a real differentiator. But a differentiator only differentiates if the buyer can see it during the part of the process where they're actually choosing. A rep armed with a great POSE story is solving a problem the buyer stopped having two-thirds of the way through their research. If nearly half of first-time buyers already have a preferred vendor in mind before they show any measurable intent, and two-thirds would rather never talk to a rep at all, the shortlist is usually locked before the call gets booked. You don't sell your way out of commodity treatment in the fraction of the funnel where you still get a turn. Published, not performed Here's the reframe. Value that isn't published doesn't exist, as far as the buyer's research is concerned. It doesn't matter if your veteran rep can rattle off cross-references, explain a substitution three ways, or quote a real ETA off the top of her head. If none of that lives on the product page, a buyer comparing five distributors' catalogs sees five lists of parts and five prices. The rep's expertise is real. It's also invisible to most of the process. What the veteran rep knows What the product page usually shows Which three SKUs cross-reference to a discontinued part A part number and a price Real-world lead time vs. the ERP's default promise date "In stock" or nothing Which spec sheet actually matches this application A generic manufacturer PDF, if any What substitution won't void the warranty Nothing — that's a phone call Every row on the right is a place a buyer defaults to price because nothing else was offered. That's not the buyer being cheap. That's the buyer optimizing over the only variable you gave them. The AI layer doesn't forgive this, it punishes it harder If a thin PDP loses you a human buyer's attention, it loses you an AI answer engine's citation outright. Structured, entity-rich content isn't a nice-to-have for discoverability anymore. Pages with advanced structured data report 3.2x more answer-engine citations on competitive queries, and 68% of pages cited in Google's AI Overviews carry structured markup, per recent analysis of citation patterns. An AI system answering "which distributor stocks this part with same-week delivery" isn't calling your rep to ask. It's reading your markup, or it's reading someone else's. This is the part the sales-culture framing misses. The audience for your value proposition no longer only includes humans who might eventually accept a phone call. It now includes a retrieval system that will quote whichever distributor's structured data actually answers the question, whether or not that distributor has the better rep. What the field actually shows We built the Top Distributors 2026 index , scoring 200+ distributors across six operating archetypes, to test this against real sites instead of survey sentiment. The Digital Readiness Index behind it measures 14 signals across four pillars, all pulled from each distributor's own live pages: spec completeness, cross-reference depth, technical documentation, structured markup. The pattern holds. The distributors scoring high aren't the ones with the best sales training decks. They're the ones whose product pages read like the conversation a good rep would have, with spec depth, substitution logic, and availability sitting in the page's own data instead of locked in someone's head. That's the actual fix, and it's a publishing problem before it's a selling problem. Your PIM already stores most of what your best rep knows. It's just sitting in fields nobody enriched, mapped to a template nobody finished. Anglera's job is closing that gap, turning what's stranded in the PIM into what's actually live on the page, so the value your team already has stops being invisible to the majority of the buying journey that never asks a human at all.

title: Connecting a global workforce: Jose U.’s career at Cummins Inc. | Cummins Inc.
summary: Learn more about Connecting a global workforce: Jose U.’s career at Cummins Inc. from Cummins, Inc., an industry leader in reliable power solutions for more than 100 years.
body_text: Connecting a global workforce: Jose U.’s career at Cummins Inc. By Cummins Inc., Global Power Technology Leader Jul 07, 2026 At Cummins Inc., connection goes beyond collaboration. It is about creating an environment where employees across countries, languages and cultures feel seen, supported and empowered to do meaningful work. For Jose U., a Senior Project Coordinator based in Nashville, Tennessee, that belief has shaped both his personal journey and his career at Cummins. “I’ve been with Cummins for eight years as of February 2026,” Jose said. “Looking back, every stop along the way helped prepare me for where I am today.” A global perspective shaped through experience Jose’s journey began in Honduras, where he grew up before moving to the United States to study Communications and Public Relations at the University of South Alabama. “College was a defining time for me,” he said. “Those experiences taught me how to connect with people from all walks of life, adapt quickly and balance creativity with hard work.” After graduating, he returned to Honduras to teach English before transitioning into marketing and advertising. His work included public relations campaigns, creative projects and global brands, helping him refine his ability to communicate across industries and audiences. “I had the chance to work on a wide variety of creative projects,” he said. “Those experiences helped me build confidence and learn how to communicate in meaningful ways.” In 2012, Jose relocated to Nashville, where he built experience in advertising, sales and account management. While his path was not linear, each step strengthened his ability to connect with people. “My career has never been a straight line and I think that’s what makes it meaningful,” he said. “Every experience helped shape the empathy and people-first mindset that guide me today.” Finding purpose at Cummins In 2018, Jose joined Cummins as a bilingual Customer Order Management Analyst, a role that marked a turning point in his career. “That opportunity completely changed the direction of my career,” he said. The company’s global reach initially caught his attention, but a personal connection made the opportunity even more meaningful. “I remember seeing a Cummins calendar at my dad’s workplace when I was younger,” he said. “At the time, I never imagined I would build a career here. Now, it means a lot knowing how proud he is.” Across every role, Jose has remained focused on communication as a way to connect people across cultures. “As someone who learned to navigate new environments in my second language, I’ve always valued communication, adaptability and making people feel understood,” he said. Supporting a global workforce through communication Early in his Cummins career, Jose supported distributors across Latin America and the Caribbean, gaining experience in global operations and cross-cultural communication. “That experience taught me how important it is to understand different communication styles and build strong relationships,” he said. In 2022, he transitioned to the Translation Services team as a Senior Project Coordinator. Today, he supports communication across languages and regions, helping ensure employees worldwide have access to clear, accurate information. His work includes video translation, ASL interpretation coordination, eLearning localization, document translation and multilingual communication initiatives. “At the heart of it all, my role is about helping people connect,” he said. “It is about making sure employees across the globe feel informed, included and supported.” Creating impact through employee experience For Jose, success is measured by the impact communication has on employees. “One of the most rewarding parts of my job is receiving positive feedback after a project is completed,” he said. “It’s a reminder that communication matters and that even behind the scenes, our work can make someone’s day easier.” He sees equitable communication as essential to building an inclusive workplace. “Every culture deserves the same level of respect, support and communication, no matter where they are located,” he said. He also values the collaboration behind that work. “We may be a small team but we accomplish a tremendous amount together,” he said. “We’re constantly finding creative ways to support a global workforce.” A culture of belonging and inclusion Jose describes the culture at Cummins as inclusive, supportive and people focused. “From day one, I’ve felt like I belong here,” he said. “It’s an environment where learning is encouraged and employees are reminded that they matter.” Beyond his day-to-day role, Jose has helped create opportunities for connection. He led GOAL Nashville, the company’s Latino affinity group, for three years and founded the Right Environment Committee at his site in 2026. “I’ve always enjoyed bringing people together,” he said. “Creating spaces where people feel supported and connected really matters.” As an immigrant, inclusion is deeply personal. “I understand how important it is for people from different backgrounds to feel respected and represented,” he said. “I carry that mindset into everything I do.” Resilience and the power of support In 2023, Jose faced a life-changing challenge when he was diagnosed with a brain tumor and underwent a 13-hour surgery. “It was one of the scariest moments my family and I have ever faced,” he said. During his recovery, the support he received from colleagues reinforced the company’s culture. “The kindness and encouragement I received made me feel seen, valued and supported,” he said. “In moments like that, you find out what kind of people surround you.” His team stepped in to support him without hesitation. “My manager showed incredible compassion and my team carried my workload while I focused on healing,” he said. That experience reshaped his perspective. “It reminded me that behind every project and deadline are people who truly care about one another.” Growth and opportunity at Cummins Throughout his career, Jose has grown through both his role and involvement in employee-led initiatives, strengthening his leadership, communication and creativity. “These experiences allowed me to make a meaningful impact on the people around me,” he said. He remains focused on continuing to learn and grow. “Cummins has taught me that growth does not always happen in a straight line,” he said. “If you stay open to opportunities, the sky is the limit.” Staying grounded and giving advice to others Outside of work, Jose expresses his creativity through music as a member of the Nashville-based band Pretty Ravens. He also enjoys film, live music and spending time with family. “Staying connected to my roots and the people I love keeps me grounded,” he said. For those considering a career at Cummins, his advice is simple. “Don’t think twice about it,” he said. “This is a place where you can grow into the best version of yourself.” He encourages candidates to stay curious and embrace collaboration. “If you come in willing to learn and be a good teammate, the opportunities are endless,” he said. He adds one final reflection. “ We Are Cummins is more than a phrase,” he said. “After my experience here, I can honestly say those words truly mean something.” Author Profiles Cummins Inc., Global Power Technology Leader Cummins Inc., a global power leader, is committed to powering a more prosperous world. Since 1919, we have delivered innovative solutions that move people, goods and economies forward. Our five business segments—Engine, Components, Distribution, Power Systems and Accelera™ by Cummins—offer a broad portfolio, including advanced diesel, electric and hybrid powertrains; integrated power generation systems; critical components such as aftertreatment, turbochargers, fuel systems, controls, transmissions, axles and brakes; and zero-emissions technologies like battery and electric powertrain systems. With a global footprint, deep technical expertise and an extensive service network, we deliver dependable, cutting-edge solutions tailored to our customers’ needs, supporting them through the energy transition with our Destination Zero strategy. We create value for customers, investors and employees and strengthen communities through our corporate responsibility global priorities: education, equity and environment. Headquartered in Columbus, Indiana, Cummins employs approximately 67,400 people worldwide and earned $2.8 billion on $33.7 billion in sales in 2025. Introducing the Bretton AI-native managed service
summary: Introducing the Bretton AI-native managed service. Hand us your managed service contract, and we transform it into an AI-native program. Priced on outcomes rather than headcount, get a true win-win-win: advance your AI agenda, comply with new regulatory expectations, all while your operations costs come down.
body_text: Having spent twenty five years working for and with financial institutions, one constant I’ve encountered time and again is that the cost of compliance goes up every year. The reason is simple. Business growth means more transactions, more alerts, and more headcount. Bad actors are coming up with new ways to conduct crimes. Regulators are constantly putting pressure by scrutinizing operations. To combat these rising costs, financial institutions have increasingly moved to outsourcing and offshoring. Today's managed service providers are in a bind. Their contracts are priced by the hour or by the alert, so either way revenue rises with volume, and a provider whose revenue scales with the work has little reason to shrink it. Providers know their clients want lower costs, but with few genuine options to cut spend without cutting corners, offshoring becomes the default lever. Unfortunately, this isn't great for their end customers, as the incentives aren't aligned. While offshoring does lower the labor rate, the savings rarely survive quality expectations and raise the regulatory risk to the program. What the FinCEN proposal changes On April 7, 2026, FinCEN, with the FDIC, OCC, and NCUA, proposed the most significant reform to how these programs are judged in a generation. It is still a proposed rule, but the direction is clear. It moves compliance away from process and volume toward effectiveness and outcomes: put the best resources against real risk, spend less on the low-risk activity that has filled queues for years, and keep an experienced, US-based team for the hardest cases. It also encourages the use of innovative tools such as artificial intelligence and views the adoption of new technologies as a positive factor. The question is shifting from how many alerts did you review to how well did your program address your actual risk. That is the question good operators always wanted to be judged on. For my entire career the incentives pointed the other way. Now they are starting to line up. Introducing the Bretton AI-native managed service Bretton is pioneering this superior approach for everyone. Hand us your managed service contract, and we transform it into an AI-native program. Priced on outcomes rather than headcount, get a true win-win-win: advance your AI agenda, comply with new regulatory expectations, all while your operations costs come down. AI supports a majority of your operations with a human-in-the-loop throughout, while Bretton's experienced SMEs handle change management, quality control, and program development. You get the leverage of technology and the oversight that only industry veterans can deliver. Our forward deployed engineers build, train, and tune the AI to match your program, so you adopt AI without the capital investment, and the more efficient we make the operation, the better your outcomes. Our industry experts provide human intelligence to disposition alerts focusing on quality outcomes providing the optimized balance of technology and human operations. Why I joined Bretton AI To me, this issue matters far beyond cost. Compliance has always been a constraint on who a bank can serve, and every dollar and hour locked in the back office is a customer the institution cannot reach. For twenty five years I watched that cost only rise. This is the first time I have seen a real opportunity to bring it down materially, and to do so while advancing an AI agenda in a controlled, human-in-the-loop way. If you run compliance, risk, financial crimes or fraud operations, I would like to talk. Grow the bank. Not the back office.
